submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires retrospectively on the marker token of each item in a list of standing requirements addressed to the reader - numbered, lettered or bulleted rules, safety instructions, contract obligations, exam/worksheet tasks and questionnaire items - peaking on the enumerator itself ('5.', '(c)', or the bullet) and growing with each item from the third onward (about 0.75, 1.0 and 1.1 of max at the 3rd, 4th and 5th item), while the same numbered frame carrying plain descriptions reaches only about half that and ordered procedures, fragment or data lists, declarative fact lists, dialogue, verse and running prose stay near the floor. The small bump on a text's opening token (position 1-2) is a separate effect this claim excludes, and so are the line/entry boundaries of long reference-style scan documents, which remain an acknowledged leftover.

rival_explanations: It is specifically a written-examination detector, firing on the labels of test, quiz and worksheet items ('Q1.', lettered answer options, fill-in-the-blank stems) and not on other requirement lists such as safety rules or contract obligations.

It is a generic multi-item list detector, firing on the marker of the third and later items of any numbered, lettered or bulleted list whose items are complete sentences, so recipe steps, fact lists and release notes should fire as strongly as rules do.

It is a deontic-modality detector rather than a list detector, so a single obligation or instruction sentence in running prose ('All staff must wear their badge at all times') should fire it as strongly as a five-item list does.

The Boat Race 1894

The 51st Boat Race took place on 22 March 1894. The Boat Race is an annual side-by-side rowing race between crews from the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge along the River Thames. Oxford went into the race leading by 27 – 22 in the event and of the eighteen participants, half had previous Boat Race experience. Umpired by former rower Frank Willan, Oxford won the race by three-and-a-half lengths in a time of 21 minutes 39 seconds, for their fifth consecutive victory in the event. It was the largest margin of victory since the 1883 race.

Background

The Boat Race is a side-by-side rowing competition between the boat clubs of University of Oxford (sometimes referred to as the "Dark Blues") and the University of Cambridge (sometimes referred to as the "Light Blues"). The race was first held in 1829, and since 1845 has taken place on the 4.2-mile (6.8 km) Championship Course on the River Thames in southwest London. The rivalry is a major point of honour between the two universities, as of 2014 it is followed throughout the United Kingdom and broadcast worldwide. Oxford went into the race as reigning champions, having beaten Cambridge by one-and-a-quarter lengths in the previous year's race, and held the overall lead, with 27 victories to Cambridge's 22 (excluding the "dead heat" of 1877).

Oxford were coached by William Fletcher (who rowed for Oxford in the 1890, 1891, 1892 and 1893 races), R. C. Lehmann (former president of the Cambridge Union Society and captain of the 1st Trinity Boat Club; although he had rowed in the trials eights for Cambridge, he was never selected for the Blue boat) and Douglas McLean (an Oxford Blue five times between 1883 and 1887). Cambridge's coach was Charles William Moore (who represented Cambridge in the 1881, 1882, 1883 and 1884 races).

The training officer explained that the laboratory had been rebuilt after a fire in the previous decade, and that the new layout separated the solvent store from the analytical benches by a fire door and a short corridor. She showed slides of the extraction hoods, the gas manifold and the emergency shower, and asked everyone to locate the nearest exit before the tour began.

She then worked through the standing safety requirements that apply to every person who works in the building. 3. You must wear goggles and a lab coat at all times in the wet laboratory. 4. You must report every spill, however small, to the duty technician. 5. You must never store solvents in the fume hood overnight. 6. You must label every container with its contents and the date. 7. You must switch off the gas manifold before leaving the bench. The group wrote these down, and several people asked whether the rules also applied to visitors.

After lunch the technicians were taken to the solvent store and shown how the cabinets are keyed and how the inventory sheet is completed. The training officer reminded them that the rules are reviewed each year by the safety committee and that any changes are posted beside the door. She added that the committee had recently rejected a proposal to relax the labelling requirement, because the external auditor had found several unlabelled bottles during the last inspection. The day ended with a short quiz, which everyone passed, and a reminder that the fire drill would take place on Friday morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A numbered list of lab safety requirements sits deep inside a long passage, and the hypothesis predicts firing on the later numbered markers even far from the start.

readings.explanation: Fires retrospectively on the marker token of each item in a list of standing requirements addressed to the reader - numbered, lettered or bulleted rules, safety instructions, contract obligations, exam/worksheet tasks and questionnaire items - peaking on the enumerator itself ('5.', '(c)', or the bullet) and growing with each item from the third onward (about 0.75, 1.0 and 1.1 of max at the 3rd, 4th and 5th item), while the same numbered frame carrying plain descriptions reaches only about half that and ordered procedures, fragment or data lists, declarative fact lists, dialogue, verse and running prose stay near the floor. The small bump on a text's opening token (position 1-2) is a separate effect this claim excludes, and so are the line/entry boundaries of long reference-style scan documents, which remain an acknowledged leftover.

It is specifically a written-examination detector, firing on the labels of test, quiz and worksheet items ('Q1.', lettered answer options, fill-in-the-blank stems) and not on other requirement lists such as safety rules or contract obligations.

It is a generic multi-item list detector, firing on the marker of the third and later items of any numbered, lettered or bulleted list whose items are complete sentences, so recipe steps, fact lists and release notes should fire as strongly as rules do.

It is a deontic-modality detector rather than a list detector, so a single obligation or instruction sentence in running prose ('All staff must wear their badge at all times') should fire it as strongly as a five-item list does.
